items.text: Arbitration with or without intervention of court

segments.text: Arbitration is a method of resolving a dispute outside ordinary court adjudication by referring it to an agreed neutral decision-maker called an arbitrator.

Study the arbitration agreement, appointment of arbitrator, reference of dispute, award, and the limited situations in which a court becomes involved. The key idea is party choice: parties agree to submit a dispute to arbitration, while courts may support or supervise the process according to law.

Arbitration is consensual adjudication. The parties agree that an identified dispute, or disputes of a defined class, will be decided by an arbitrator or arbitral tribunal rather than by an ordinary court as the primary decision-maker. The arbitration agreement is therefore the source of arbitral authority, while the award is the tribunal’s determination of the dispute.

In Pakistan, the traditional domestic statutory framework remains associated with the Arbitration Act, 1940. A student should distinguish domestic arbitration under that framework from international commercial arbitration and from the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards, which may involve separate legislation and treaty obligations.

The process can be learned as a sequence: a valid arbitration agreement exists; a dispute falls within its scope; the tribunal is constituted; jurisdictional or procedural objections are addressed; each side presents its case and evidence; the tribunal renders an award; and the award may then be recognized, enforced, remitted or challenged only within the legal framework governing the arbitration.

Party autonomy is important, but it is not unlimited. Mandatory law may determine whether a dispute is arbitrable, whether minimum procedural fairness was observed, and on what grounds a court may intervene.

Court support and court supervision should be kept conceptually separate. A court may support arbitration by staying parallel litigation, assisting with appointment in circumstances specified by law, preserving the process, or enforcing the award. Supervision concerns the limited grounds on which an award or arbitral process may be reviewed. The central principle is that a court does not ordinarily rehear the entire merits merely because one party dislikes the result.

This explains why the phrase 'alternative dispute resolution' should not be taken to mean 'law-free dispute resolution'. Arbitration operates within a legal framework that gives effect to the parties’ agreement and protects minimum procedural standards.

Hypothetical illustration: two companies include an arbitration clause in a supply contract. A payment dispute later arises. If one company files an ordinary suit despite the clause, the other may invoke the arbitration agreement and seek the relief available under the applicable arbitration law. The legal question is not simply which forum is more convenient; it is whether the dispute falls within a valid arbitration agreement and what the governing statute permits the court to do.

items.text: Think of arbitration as a private decision-making process created by the parties' agreement. The agreement is the legal foundation of the arbitrator's authority.

valid arbitration agreement, dispute arises, arbitrator is appointed, parties present their case, the arbitrator gives an award, and the award may then require recognition or enforcement through the legal system.

Court involvement does not convert arbitration into an ordinary civil suit. Courts generally perform supporting or supervisory functions where the law allows, such as appointment-related assistance, stay of proceedings, or review of an award on limited grounds.
In an exam, distinguish the arbitration agreement from the award: the agreement sends disputes to arbitration; the award is the final decision of the arbitrator on the dispute.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not describe arbitration as completely independent of courts. It is private adjudication, but legislation defines the circumstances in which courts may assist or supervise.

items.text: agreement → reference → proceedings → award → court enforcement/challenge.
Prepare the difference between arbitration with court intervention and arbitration without initial court intervention.
Read the relevant Arbitration Act provisions together with illustrations or decided examples.

segments.text: Answer through a process diagram and clearly separate the role of the arbitrator from the role of the court.
The arbitrator decides the dispute and gives an award.
Courts may assist in appointment, stay proceedings, remit/modify/set aside where law permits, and enforce an award.
Arbitration aims at a comparatively flexible dispute-resolution process.
